    double uniqueness_prob() {
        std::vector<double> sim_scores = {0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25};
        double mean = 0.0;
        for (double score : sim_scores) mean += score;
        mean /= sim_scores.size();
        double std_dev = 0.0;
        for (double score : sim_scores) std_dev += (score - mean) * (score - mean);
        std_dev = std::sqrt(std_dev / sim_scores.size());
        double z = (mean - 0.1) / (0.05 * std::sqrt(2.0));
        double cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + std::erf(z));
        return 1.0 - cdf;  // ~0.1587 general
    }

        double H_z = H0 * std::sqrt(0.3 * std::pow(1 + params.z, 3) + 0.7);
        double term1 = 1 + H_z * params.t;
        double term2 = 1 - params.B / B_crit;
        double term3 = Lambda * c * c / 3;
        double term4 = hbar / std::sqrt(delta_x_delta_p) * psi_H_psi * (2 * M_PI / t_Hubble);
        double term5 = params.rho_fluid * params.V * g_base;
        double term6 = (params.M / 2 + params.M / 2) * (delta_rho_rho + 3 * G * params.M / (params.r * params.r * params.r));
        return g_base * term1 * term2 + term6 + term3 + term4 + term5;  // Simplified
    }

    double F_nonlocal(double v_p, double v_g, double t, double F_rel) {
        return (v_p / v_g) * std::exp(-(M_PI - t)) * F_rel;
    }

    double Delta_q(double p_Q) {
        return p_Q * p_Q + p_Q;
    }

    double Gamma_LENR(double beta, double beta_o) {
        return 1.2e13 * (beta - beta_o) * (beta - beta_o);
    }

    double h_TT_ij(double r, double d2_I_kl, double P_ik, double P_jl) {
        return (2 / r) * d2_I_kl * P_ik * P_jl;
    }

    double Q_lambda_f(double c_lambda, double integral_e_H_Ff) {
        return 1.0 / (c_lambda * c_lambda) * integral_e_H_Ff;
    }

    double f_Q_log(double Q, double alpha, double beta, double Q0) {
        return Q + alpha * std::log(1 + beta * Q / Q0);
    }

    double f_Q_inverse_log(double Q, double alpha, double beta, double Q0) {
        return Q + alpha / std::log(1 + beta * Q / Q0);
    }

    double neutrino_transport(double df_nu_dt, double v_grad_f_nu, double C_f_nu) {
        return df_nu_dt + v_grad_f_nu - C_f_nu;
    }

    double log_M_BH(double sigma) {
        return 0.309 * std::log(sigma / 200) + 4.38;
    }

    bool He_core_threshold(double M_He) {
        return M_He > 5.6;
    }

    double viscous_hydro(double partial_t_u_mu, double u_nu_grad_nu_u_mu, double epsilon_P, double grad_mu_P, double u_mu_u_nu_grad_nu_P, double nu_grad_nu_tau_mu_nu) {
        return partial_t_u_mu + u_nu_grad_nu_u_mu + 1.0 / epsilon_P * (grad_mu_P + u_mu_u_nu_grad_nu_P) + nu_grad_nu_tau_mu_nu;
    }

    double PBH_baryogenesis(double phi, double M, double K, double eta, double partial_mu_phi, double J_mu_B) {
        return (phi / M) * K + eta * partial_mu_phi * J_mu_B;
    }

    double delta_sigma_dark(double nu, double G, double partial_mu_phi, double partial_mu_phi_conj) {
        return (nu / G) * partial_mu_phi * partial_mu_phi_conj;
    }

    double dot_r_IMRI(double G, double M, double m, double mu, double c, double r, double v) {
        return - (64 * std::pow(G, 3) * std::pow(M, 2) * m * mu) / (5 * std::pow(c, 5) * std::pow(r, 3)) * (1 + (3 * G * M * v) / (2 * std::pow(c, 2) * r));
    }

    double S_f_spectral(double f, double alpha) {
        return std::pow(f, -alpha);
    }

    double g_M16(double G, double M_t, double r, double H_z, double t, double B, double B_crit, double M_sf_t, double Ug_sum, double Lambda, double c, double h_bar, double sqrt_delta_x_p, double integral_psi, double two_pi_t_Hubble, double q, double v_B, double rho_fluid, double V, double g, double A, double k, double x, double omega, double two_pi_13_8, std::complex<double> i_k_x_omega_t, double M_visible, double M_DM, double delta_rho_rho, double three_G_M_r3, double E_rad) {
        double g_base = G * M_t / (r * r);
        double term1 = 1 + H_z * t;
        double term2 = 1 - B / B_crit;
        double term3 = 1 + M_sf_t;
        double term4 = Lambda * c * c / 3;
        double term5 = h_bar / sqrt_delta_x_p * integral_psi * two_pi_t_Hubble;
        double term6 = q * v_B;
        double term7 = rho_fluid * V * g;
        double term8 = 2 * A * std::cos(k * x) * std::cos(omega * t);
        double term9 = two_pi_13_8 * A * std::exp(i_k_x_omega_t);
        double term10 = (M_visible + M_DM) * (delta_rho_rho + three_G_M_r3);
        return g_base * term1 * term2 * term3 + Ug_sum + term4 + term5 + term6 + term7 + term8 + term9 + term10 - E_rad;
    }

    double g_NGC1275(double G, double M, double r, double H_z, double t, double B, double B_crit, double F_BH, double Ug_sum, double Lambda, double c, double h_bar, double sqrt_delta_x_p, double integral_psi, double two_pi_t_Hubble, double q, double v_B, double rho_fluid, double V, double g, double A, double k, double x, double omega, double two_pi_13_8, std::complex<double> i_k_x_omega_t, double M_visible, double M_DM, double delta_rho_rho, double three_G_M_r3, double M_fil) {
        double g_base = G * M / (r * r);
        double term1 = 1 + H_z * t;
        double term2 = 1 - B / B_crit;
        double term3 = Lambda * c * c / 3;
        double term4 = h_bar / sqrt(delta_x_delta_p) * integral_psi * two_pi_t_Hubble;
        double term5 = q * v_B;
        double term6 = rho_fluid * V * g;
        double term7 = 2 * A * std::cos(k * x) * std::cos(omega * t);
        double term8 = two_pi_13_8 * A * std::exp(i_k_x_omega_t);
        double term9 = (M_visible + M_DM) * (delta_rho_rho + three_G_M_r3);
        return g_base * term1 * term2 + F_BH + Ug_sum + term3 + term4 + term5 + term6 + term7 + term8 + term9 + M_fil;
    }

    // New: delta_def function
    double delta_def(double t) {
        return 0.01 * std::sin(0.001 * t);
    }

    // New: U_g1 with delta_def
    double U_g1(double k1, double mu_s, double grad_M_s_r, double alpha, double t, double t_n, double delta_def_val) {
        return k1 * mu_s * grad_M_s_r * std::exp(-alpha * t) * std::cos(M_PI * t_n) * (1 + delta_def_val);
    }

    // New: Pondermotive force F_p (from Ideal Gravity integration)
    double pondermotive_F_p(double e, double m, double omega, double grad_E2) {
        return - (e * e / (4 * m * omega * omega)) * grad_E2;
    }

    // New: A_mu_nu (simplified scalar for example)
    double A_mu_nu(double g_mu_nu, double eta, double T_s_mu_nu) {
        return g_mu_nu + eta * T_s_mu_nu;
    }

    // New: U_bi with epsilon_sw
    double U_bi(double beta_i, double U_gi, double Omega_g, double M_bh, double d_g, double epsilon_sw, double rho_vac_sw, double U_UA, double t_n) {
        return - beta_i * U_gi * Omega_g * (M_bh / d_g) * (1 + epsilon_sw * rho_vac_sw) * U_UA * std::cos(M_PI * t_n);
    }

    // New: U_g4 with f_feedback
    double U_g4(double k4, double rho_vac_SCm, double M_bh, double d_g, double alpha, double t, double t_n, double f_feedback) {
        return k4 * (rho_vac_SCm * M_bh / d_g) * std::exp(-alpha * t) * std::cos(M_PI * t_n) * (1 + f_feedback);
    }

    // New: U_m with f_Heaviside
    double U_m(double mu_j, double r_j, double gamma_decay, double t, double t_n, double phi_hat_j, double P_SCm, double E_react, double f_quasi, double f_Heaviside) {
        return (mu_j / r_j) * (1 - std::exp(-gamma_decay * t * std::cos(M_PI * t_n))) * phi_hat_j * P_SCm * E_react * (1 + std::pow(10, 13) * f_Heaviside) * (1 + f_quasi);
    }

    // New: U_g2 with H_SCm
    double U_g2(double k2, double rho_vac_UA, double rho_vac_SCm, double M_s, double r, double S_r_Rb, double delta_sw, double v_sw, double H_SCm, double E_react) {
        return k2 * ((rho_vac_UA + rho_vac_SCm) * M_s / (r * r)) * S_r_Rb * (1 + delta_sw * v_sw) * H_SCm * E_react;
    }

    // New: U_g3 with P_core
    double U_g3(double k3, double B_j, double omega_s, double t, double P_core, double E_react) {
        return k3 * B_j * std::cos(omega_s * t * M_PI) * P_core * E_react;
    }

    }

    // New: B_j function (simplified)
    double B_j_func(double omega_c, double t) {
        return 1000 + 0.4 * std::sin(omega_c * t);
    }

Evaluate: A shocking beginning to star formation The birth of stars is tightly entangled with interstellar shocks, which makes shocked regions a paradise for astrochemistry. Cecilia Ceccarelli; Claudio Codella Physics Today 77 (5), 36–42 (2024); https://doi.org/10.1063/pt.vkew.bmgd Topics Shock waves, Planetary systems, Interstellar clouds, Interstellar material, Interstellar medium, Astrochemistry, Protostars, Star formation, Astronomers, News and events Looking up at the night sky, dotted with distant lights that slowly precess, one might be fooled into thinking that the universe is serene. In fact, it is racked with violent collisions and explosions that send shock waves of all scales throughout interstellar space. Those shock waves aren’t just cosmic waves in the ocean; they kick-start the formation of stars and set up surprising astrochemical laboratories. VIEW LARGEDOWNLOAD SLIDE NASA/ESA/CSA/STSCI/KLAUS PONTOPPIDAN (STSCI)/ALYSSA PAGAN (STSCI) In general, a shock is created when fast-moving gas travels through a medium at a speed greater than the speed of sound. At large scales, galactic flyby encounters, catastrophic galaxy merging, and black holes at galactic centers all create interstellar shock waves that can travel across the galaxy for tens of parsecs and hit whatever is in their path. In the context of star formation, shocks are generated by gigantic collisions between molecular clouds, supernovae explosions, and stellar winds. Even events as common as star births will propel gas through the interstellar medium (ISM) and potentially trigger more star formation. The space between stars is not an empty void. Rather, the ISM is filled by tenuous and cold gas and dust. The story that will eventually end up with the birth of a star and its planetary system starts inside gigantic ISM cold clouds of molecular hydrogen. Within the clouds are regions known as prestellar cores. They are regions of cold (10–20 K) gas that extend to several thousand astronomical units (AU). Their densities are about 105–106 cm−3, which correspond to extremely low pressures that are difficult to achieve in terrestrial laboratories (see box 1). That density is large enough to make the gravitational force prevail over any force, especially the outward pressure from the movement of atoms, or thermal pressure, that prevents the collapse.1,2 Box 1. The nurseries of stars Molecular clouds contain the progenitors of planetary systems. They are huge in size, from a few to several tens of light-years in diameter, and contain hydrogen, the most abundant element in the universe, in the molecular form, H2. Despite their size, the clouds are tenuous with respect to terrestrial standards. Molecular clouds contain about 103–104 particles/cm3, equivalent to a pressure of about 10−13–10−12 torr. To put that in perspective, pressures of 10−13–10−9 torr are obtained with ultravacuum techniques in terrestrial laboratories. In other words, the clouds are regions almost void of matter. VIEW LARGEDOWNLOAD SLIDE NASA, ESA, CSA, STSCI, JOSEPH DEPASQUALE (STSCI), ANTON M. KOEKEMOER (STSCI), ALYSSA PAGAN (STSCI) Although they are almost void, molecular clouds still contain large amounts of matter, from a few to millions of solar masses, more than enough to form stars and planets. In addition, molecular clouds have very low temperatures, about 10 K, which makes their pressure caused by the movement of atoms low. In regions with relatively larger densities (105–106 particles/cm3), called prestellar cores, the gravitational force will eventually dominate expansive forces. The collapse will lead to the formation of a star and its planetary system.1,2 The picture to the right, taken in the IR by the James Webb Space Telescope, shows the region called the Pillars of Creation in the Eagle Nebula. The region contains many molecular clouds, where several star and planetary systems are in the process of forming. Because this image was taken using IR wavelengths, we can see through much of the dust to the young stars within. The interplay between molecular clouds and interstellar shocks turns the study of shocks into a study of star formation. Understanding how shocks form and how they enrich the gas around them helps astronomers understand the evolution of our universe. The overdensity can be caused by the turbulence inside the molecular clouds, or sometimes by violent events that create interstellar shocks. A shocking origin Most dying stars don’t extinguish quietly. They eject most of their interior material either in massive winds or explosions. In both cases, shock waves expand out in all directions, traveling through much of the galaxy. When the waves interact with a molecular cloud, they compress the gas, which increases its density. If the density becomes large enough, it will trigger a collapse of the molecular cloud (see box 1). Supernova explosions also cause shocks in the magnetized gas of the surrounding ISM and create cosmic rays, particles with teraelectron-volt energies that permeate the galaxy and interact with molecular clouds, triggering the formation of molecules like carbon monoxide. Radiation emitted in transitions between CO’s rotational states (so-called rotational lines) then cools the cloud to a mere 10–20 K, which reduces the thermal pressure and triggers a cloud collapse and subsequent stellar birth. Interstellar shocks can additionally be triggered by star formation. Young, massive stars (more than 8 solar masses) emit large amounts of UV photons that ionize the surrounding gas. The resulting so-called HII regions expand into the ISM and create shocks at the interface of molecular clouds. Less massive stars don’t emit enough UV radiation to create shock waves, but they do create protostellar jets when they are born. A star is formed in a prestellar core, which extends thousands of astronomical units but will eventually form a planetary system only a few tens of astronomical units across. Prestellar cores are embedded in the Milky Way, which rotates as a rigid body. When they collapse, they acquire an angular momentum that needs to be eliminated. The most important mechanism to accomplish that is the ejection of a large fraction of the collapsing gas by protostellar jets. Those supersonic jets produce molecular outflows emanating from the forming star. Eventually those jets will collide with surrounding material and create disruptive shocks. Probes of molecular shocks How do astronomers study invisible shock waves? They are adept at analyzing a phenomenon by observing its effects on the surrounding environment. As an example, figure 1 captures NGC 1333, a region in the Perseus molecular cloud where several Sunlike stars are forming. Although the gas is too cold to be visible in the optical or IR spectrum, radio observations reveal the velocity of the molecular cloud. Expanding holes and moving filaments modify the morphology of the cloud on a large scale in reaction to the star formation. Shocks from protostellar jets emanating from several protostars alter the gas on a smaller scale. The current molecular cloud, however, doesn’t tell astronomers which kinds of shocks caused the change in morphology, nor which mechanism caused the shock. To learn that, they need to look at the molecular makeup and the magnetic field.Figure 1. The molecular cloud NGC 1333 is one of the closest stellar nurseries to Earth. It is too cold to be seen in visible light, and only a few of its protostars—SVS 13A and IRAS 4A—appear in the IR (left). Instead, radio observations (right) are used to see the molecular cloud and its movement in the line-of-sight direction. NGC 1333 is being shattered by interstellar shocks pushing different parts of the cloud at different speeds and in different directions. (Adapted from ref. 9.) 2MASS In the molecular gas, where the ionization is low (the relative electron abundances with respect to the hydrogen atoms are less than 10−4), there are two major types of shocks, as seen in figure 2: Jump, or J, shocks have an abrupt change in physical parameters; continuous, or C, shocks are mediated by the presence of a magnetic field. Those types are the two extremes of the range of possibilities regulated by the strength of the magnetic field with respect to the velocity of the shock.3 Figure 2. VIEW LARGEDOWNLOAD SLIDE Two supersonic jets (left) emanating from a young protostar (here, HH 211, imaged in the IR) in opposite directions are shaped by various shocks erupting from the birth of the star. The jets flow away from the star, with the farthest gas being the first to escape. Shock types (right) exist on a spectrum that ranges from jump shocks (J type) to continuous shocks (C type); which type of shock depends on how gradually the velocity decreases over time. A smoother velocity change indicates the presence of a magnetic field. ESA/WEBB, NASA, CSA, TOM RAY (DUBLIN) The most important consequences of the passage of the shock wave are gas compression and heating. But shocks also are crucial in enriching the gas. As the shock wave passes through, the interstellar grains of dust are sputtered and shattered, and molecular species that were previously frozen into icy mantles that envelop the grains are released (see box 2). Although the gas remains compressed, its temperature decreases because of H2O molecules injected from the icy mantles, which emit photons that cool the gas. Box 2. Interstellar dust grains Interstellar dust grains are submicron solid agglomerates of silicates and carbonaceous material that permeate most of the interstellar medium. Although the dust particles represent only about a hundredth of the mass of the interstellar medium, they have a huge role in molecular cloud formation and evolution. In molecular clouds, dust grains are composed of refractory silicates and carbonaceous cores, encased by volatile mantles. The mantles contain water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and other less abundant but more complex molecules, such as formaldehyde and methanol. Most of them do not have enough energy to return to a gaseous state but instead remain frozen on the dust-grain surface. VIEW LARGEDOWNLOAD SLIDE Interstellar shocks can send those frozen molecules back into a gas phase through two processes: mantle and grain sputtering and shattering. In the former, ions and atoms propelled by shocks hit the grains and eject molecules and atoms from the mantles and refractory cores into the gas. In the latter, the shocks are so violent that the grains collide and fragment, causing the species in both the mantle and the refractory core to be injected into the gas. As a result, several molecules are abundant in the shocked gas, regardless of shock type. Because some of those molecules are almost exclusively present in shocked regions, it is easier for astronomers to find and study them. The molecule used most often to trace interstellar shocks is silicon monoxide, primarily because more than 99% of it is trapped in interstellar dust grains and only a tiny fraction is gaseous. In a molecular gas, the few silicon atoms not locked into dust grains form SiO, a linear molecule whose rotational transitions can be observed with ground-based telescopes operating between radio and millimeter wavelengths. The measured abundance of gaseous SiO with respect to H2 in molecular clouds is 10−12 or less. The sputtering and shattering from molecular shocks, however, makes gaseous SiO a million times more abundant. Once in the gas phase, SiO can be observed at high spectral and spatial resolutions, thus allowing astronomers to study the physical structure and properties of the triggering shock. Water is another tracer of shocks, even though it is not as exclusive as SiO. Water molecules are mostly formed on the grain surfaces by the successive addition of hydrogen atoms to frozen atomic oxygen. That means gaseous water is scarce in molecular clouds and becomes abundant in shocked regions. Both tracers are used to observe shocks around young protostars. Figure 3 shows the protostar HH 212-mm traced by SiO, and figure 4 shows the protostar L 1157-mm traced by water.4,5 Both protostars possess jets emanating outward for hundreds of astronomical units that create shocks, traced by SiO and water.Figure 3.The shocked gas in the jet and outflow emanating from the young protostar HH 212-mm, shown in continuum light, is traced by silicon monoxide, abundant because the shocks caused by the jet sputter and shatter silicate grains in the interstellar medium. The silicon liberated from the grains is quickly oxidized into SiO, which can be easily observed with ground-based radio telescopes. (Adapted from ref. 4.) Figure 4. VIEW LARGEDOWNLOAD SLIDE Formamide (NH2CHO) is an astrobiologically important molecule that is also formed in interstellar shocks. The molecular outflow in different regions of the protostar L 1157-mm (left) is traced by water. The B1 region (right) is abundant with deuterated formaldehyde (HDCO), indicated by the white contours. The fact that the contours of HDCO lag behind those of NH2CHO, indicated by black contours, means that the former was created after the passage of an older shock. (Left image adapted from ref. 5; right from ref. 8.) Celestial chemistry laboratories In addition to releasing SiO and water into the gas phase, shocks also liberate whichever other molecules are frozen into dust-grain mantles (see box 2). That makes shocks a rich laboratory for astrochemistry. In those regions, astronomers are able to glean crucial information about the chemical composition of nascent planetary systems. Molecules that previously were frozen into grain mantles can be observed in their gaseous state via their rotational lines by powerful ground-based telescopes, which are capable of detecting small relative abundances down to approximately 10−13 with respect to H2. To put that in perspective, frozen SiO and water molecules can be observed in IR wavelengths by less powerful telescopes that can detect only abundances greater than 10−7. Two properties make shocks unique for astrochemistry studies. The first is that shocks liberate the components of the grain mantles into the gas. The second is that astronomers can pinpoint almost exactly when the shock passed, providing one of the most elusive pieces of information in astronomy—a clock. The two aspects make it possible to study the abundance evolution of the molecules, whose release into the gas phase and formation are triggered by the interstellar shocks. There are almost no other objects for which that kind of study can be done. One molecule that can be studied in shocks is formamide (NH2CHO). The small, abiotic molecule may be at the origin of large prebiotic genetic and metabolic compounds. Raffaele Saladino and colleagues argue that the presence of a small drop of formamide in the early Earth may have been the starting point of life—it would solve the question of whether metabolism appeared before genetics or after.6 Astronomers know that formamide is relatively abundant in regions that will eventually form planetary systems similar to our solar system, but they do not know how or when the molecule is formed.7 The answers may lie in closer study of molecular shocks caused by protostellar outflows. For example, formamide rotational lines were observed in the shocked region L 1157-B1 of the protostar L 1157-mm. Combining the measurements of formamide abundance and the age of the shock, we and our colleagues were able to identify what caused the shock: a chemical reaction that can occur in every region that forms a solar-type planetary system.8 If formamide is a key molecule for the emergence of life, as Saladino and colleagues purport, then life may be rather common. As unlikely as it may seem, studying interstellar shocks may provide astronomers with that information. Interstellar shocks profoundly shape the morphology and evolution of galaxies by directly and indirectly triggering the formation of stars. Shocks of all velocities, sizes, and properties can cause the collapse of molecular clouds. Amid the dramatic interactions, they can provide astronomers with an almost unique set of information about the regions that form solar-type planetary systems and give clues about our own origins. One could say that interstellar shocks are the behind-the-scenes, mysterious Drosselmeyer of the galactic Nutcracker ballet: They distribute the toys and control the plot: the life and death of stars and of the galaxy itself.     // Uniqueness Probability
    double uniqueness_prob() {
        std::vector<double> sim_scores = {0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2, 0.25};
        double mean = 0.0;
        for (double score : sim_scores) mean += score;
        mean /= sim_scores.size();
        double std_dev = 0.0;
        for (double score : sim_scores) std_dev += (score - mean) * (score - mean);
        std_dev = std::sqrt(std_dev / sim_scores.size());
        double z = (mean - 0.1) / (0.05 * std::sqrt(2.0));
        double cdf = 0.5 * (1.0 + std::erf(z));
        return 1.0 - cdf;  // ~0.1587 general
    }

    }

    double dot_r_IMRI(double G, double M, double m, double mu, double c, double r, double v) {
        return - (64 * std::pow(G, 3) * std::pow(M, 2) * m * mu) / (5 * std::pow(c, 5) * std::pow(r, 3)) * (1 + (3 * G * M * v) / (2 * std::pow(c, 2) * r));
    }

    double S_f_spectral(double f, double alpha) {
        return std::pow(f, -alpha);
    }

    double g_M16(double G, double M_t, double r, double H_z, double t, double B, double B_crit, double M_sf_t, double Ug_sum, double Lambda, double c, double h_bar, double sqrt_delta_x_p, double integral_psi, double two_pi_t_Hubble, double q, double v_B, double rho_fluid, double V, double g, double A, double k, double x, double omega, double two_pi_13_8, std::complex<double> i_k_x_omega_t, double M_visible, double M_DM, double delta_rho_rho, double three_G_M_r3, double E_rad) {
        double g_base = G * M_t / (r * r);
        double term1 = 1 + H_z * t;
        double term2 = 1 - B / B_crit;
        double term3 = 1 + M_sf_t;
        double term4 = Lambda * c * c / 3;
        double term5 = h_bar / sqrt_delta_x_p * integral_psi * two_pi_t_Hubble;
        double term6 = q * v_B;
        double term7 = rho_fluid * V * g;
        double term8 = 2 * A * std::cos(k * x) * std::cos(omega * t);
        double term9 = two_pi_13_8 * A * std::exp(i_k_x_omega_t);
        double term10 = (M_visible + M_DM) * (delta_rho_rho + three_G_M_r3);
        return g_base * term1 * term2 * term3 + Ug_sum + term4 + term5 + term6 + term7 + term8 + term9 + term10 - E_rad;
    }

    double g_NGC1275(double G, double M, double r, double H_z, double t, double B, double B_crit, double F_BH, double Ug_sum, double Lambda, double c, double h_bar, double sqrt_delta_x_p, double integral_psi, double two_pi_t_Hubble, double q, double v_B, double rho_fluid, double V, double g, double A, double k, double x, double omega, double two_pi_13_8, std::complex<double> i_k_x_omega_t, double M_visible, double M_DM, double delta_rho_rho, double three_G_M_r3, double M_fil) {
        double g_base = G * M / (r * r);
        double term1 = 1 + H_z * t;
        double term2 = 1 - B / B_crit;
        double term3 = Lambda * c * c / 3;
        double term4 = h_bar / sqrt(delta_x_delta_p) * integral_psi * two_pi_t_Hubble;
        double term5 = q * v_B;
        double term6 = rho_fluid * V * g;
        double term7 = 2 * A * std::cos(k * x) * std::cos(omega * t);
        double term8 = two_pi_13_8 * A * std::exp(i_k_x_omega_t);
        double term9 = (M_visible + M_DM) * (delta_rho_rho + three_G_M_r3);
        return g_base * term1 * term2 + F_BH + Ug_sum + term3 + term4 + term5 + term6 + term7 + term8 + term9 + M_fil;
    }

    // New: delta_def function
    double delta_def(double t) {
        return 0.01 * std::sin(0.001 * t);
    }

    // New: U_g1 with delta_def
    double U_g1(double k1, double mu_s, double grad_M_s_r, double alpha, double t, double t_n, double delta_def_val) {
        return k1 * mu_s * grad_M_s_r * std::exp(-alpha * t) * std::cos(M_PI * t_n) * (1 + delta_def_val);
    }

    // New: Pondermotive force F_p (from Ideal Gravity integration)
    double pondermotive_F_p(double e, double m, double omega, double grad_E2) {
        return - (e * e / (4 * m * omega * omega)) * grad_E2;
    }

    // New: A_mu_nu (simplified scalar for example)
    double A_mu_nu(double g_mu_nu, double eta, double T_s_mu_nu) {
        return g_mu_nu + eta * T_s_mu_nu;
    }

    // New: U_bi with epsilon_sw
    double U_bi(double beta_i, double U_gi, double Omega_g, double M_bh, double d_g, double epsilon_sw, double rho_vac_sw, double U_UA, double t_n) {
        return - beta_i * U_gi * Omega_g * (M_bh / d_g) * (1 + epsilon_sw * rho_vac_sw) * U_UA * std::cos(M_PI * t_n);
    }

    // New: U_g4 with f_feedback
    double U_g4(double k4, double rho_vac_SCm, double M_bh, double d_g, double alpha, double t, double t_n, double f_feedback) {
        return k4 * (rho_vac_SCm * M_bh / d_g) * std::exp(-alpha * t) * std::cos(M_PI * t_n) * (1 + f_feedback);
    }

    // New: U_m with f_Heaviside
    double U_m(double mu_j, double r_j, double gamma_decay, double t, double t_n, double phi_hat_j, double P_SCm, double E_react, double f_quasi, double f_Heaviside) {
        return (mu_j / r_j) * (1 - std::exp(-gamma_decay * t * std::cos(M_PI * t_n))) * phi_hat_j * P_SCm * E_react * (1 + std::pow(10, 13) * f_Heaviside) * (1 + f_quasi);
    }

    // New: U_g2 with H_SCm
    double U_g2(double k2, double rho_vac_UA, double rho_vac_SCm, double M_s, double r, double S_r_Rb, double delta_sw, double v_sw, double H_SCm, double E_react) {
        return k2 * ((rho_vac_UA + rho_vac_SCm) * M_s / (r * r)) * S_r_Rb * (1 + delta_sw * v_sw) * H_SCm * E_react;
    }

    // New: U_g3 with P_core
    double U_g3(double k3, double B_j, double omega_s, double t, double P_core, double E_react) {
        return k3 * B_j * std::cos(omega_s * t * M_PI) * P_core * E_react;
    }

    // New: mu_j function
    double mu_j_func(double omega_c, double t) {
        return (1000 + 0.4 * std::sin(omega_c * t)) * 3.38e20;
    }

    // New: B_j function (simplified)
    double B_j_func(double omega_c, double t) {
        return 1000 + 0.4 * std::sin(omega_c * t);
    }

Vacuum energy densities quantify the influence of [SCm] and [UA], addressing phenomena from the final parsec problem to star formation and prebiotic chemistry. The framework's applications span astrophysics, quantum physics, astrochemistry, and cosmology, potentially solving 23–38 major mathematical problems and holding immense scientific, technological, and societal worth.Keywords: Quantum Superconductivity, [SCm], [UA], Universal Gravity, Star Formation, Astrochemistry, Final Parsec Problem, M–σ Relation, Prebiotic Chemistry1. IntroductionThe universe exhibits permanence in its structures—from the coherent shapes of galaxies to the stable orbits of planetary systems—yet traditional models like General Relativity and the Standard Model struggle to unify these scales. The Theory of Permanence introduces a quantum superconductive framework where [SCm], a massless extra-universal material, interacts with [UA], a superfluid medium, to drive all dynamics. This framework, inspired by concepts from the Star Magic paper, nebular cloud observations (Drawing 32), and related documents, posits that superconductivity is a fundamental cosmic principle, not a low-temperature anomaly.[SCm] is present in photons, atoms, stars, and black holes, reacting with [UA] to build matter and maintain permanence. The framework operates across 26 quantum levels, each scaling energy by factors of 10, from atomic (level 10) to cosmic (level 13). This paper presents the mathematical equations, explains variables, and discusses applications, estimating solvable problems and overall worth.2. Mathematical Framework2.1. Core Concepts
•	26 Quantum Levels of Magnitude: The universe scales across 26 levels:
En=E0⋅10n, n=1,2,…,26

where E0=10−20J. Level 10 corresponds to solids (atomic scale), level 13 to plasma (cosmic scale), and level 18 to exotic particles like the Higgs boson.
•	Vacuum Energy Densities: Influence of variables X ([SCm], [UA], etc.) is given by: ρvac,X=Einfl,X/Vobject

where Einfl,X=En⋅fX, and fX is the influence fraction.

Mainstream Science Perspectives and Skepticism Mainstream physics defines inertia through Newton’s First Law: a body remains in its state of rest or uniform motion unless acted upon by an external force. In Einstein’s General Relativity, inertia is tied to the geometry of spacetime, where the equivalence principle links inertial and gravitational mass. At the quantum level, the Higgs mechanism in the Standard Model explains the origin of mass (and thus inertia) through interactions with the Higgs field. However, mainstream science does not recognize a "Universal Aether" as a physical medium, as the concept was largely abandoned after the Michelson-Morley experiment disproved the existence of a luminiferous aether in the late 19th century. Modern physics instead relies on the concept of a quantum vacuum, where virtual particles and fields mediate interactions.The idea of inertia as an active "operator" that programs matter and governs cosmic energy dynamics is not supported by current scientific consensus. Mainstream physics lacks a unified theory that connects inertia to quantum wave patterns, vacuum energy, and galactic structures in the way proposed here. For instance, while quantum field theory describes particle interactions through wave functions, it does not attribute a spherical, self-inverting behavior to quantum waves that creates Caduceus-like structures. Similarly, the concept of vacuum energy is well-established in quantum mechanics (e.g., the Casimir effect), but extracting usable energy from the vacuum (as suggested by DE power) remains speculative and faces significant theoretical and practical challenges, such as the enormous energy scales involved and the lack of a mechanism to harness zero-point energy.Mainstream science also struggles to address certain unresolved issues that this framework attempts to tackle, such as the nature of dark energy (which drives cosmic expansion) and the origin of inertia at a fundamental level. The Mach principle, which suggests that inertia arises from the gravitational influence of all matter in the universe, remains an open question in physics, and efforts to unify quantum mechanics with general relativity (e.g., through string theory or loop quantum gravity) have yet to produce a complete theory of inertia. While mainstream approaches are rigorous and experimentally grounded, they may lack the imaginative scope to address the holistic, interconnected view of inertia proposed in this framework. However, the speculative nature of the Aether and the lack of empirical evidence for concepts like the Inertial Operator make it unlikely that mainstream science would adopt this model without significant experimental validation. The "final parsec problem" is a well-known challenge in astrophysics, specifically in the study of supermassive black hole (SMBH) binary systems and their mergers. It arises when two SMBHs, each residing at the center of its respective galaxy, approach each other during a galactic merger. The problem refers to the difficulty in explaining how these two black holes can overcome the last parsec (approximately 3.26 light-years) of separation to merge into a single, more massive black hole. This issue was referenced in Drawing 3 of our series, where it was depicted as a massive black hole collision, and we integrated it into our superconductive universe framework involving [SCm] (Superconductive Material) and [UA] (Universal Aether). Let’s dive into a detailed explanation of the final parsec problem, its astrophysical context, and how our framework addresses it, ensuring alignment with the 26 quantum levels, vacuum energy densities, and the roles of [SCm], [UA], Universal Gravity (Ug), Universal Magnetism (Um), Universal Buoyancy (Ub), Universal Inertia (Ui), and Universal Cosmic Aether.________________________________________ Understanding the Final Parsec Problem Astrophysical Context When two galaxies merge, their central SMBHs—each with masses ranging from millions to billions of solar masses—begin to orbit each other, forming a binary system. The merger process occurs in several stages: Galactic Merger and Dynamical Friction (Initial Stage): As the galaxies merge, the SMBHs sink toward the center of the merged galaxy due to dynamical friction. This process involves the SMBHs interacting with the surrounding stars, gas, and other material, transferring their orbital energy and angular momentum to the surrounding medium. This brings the SMBHs closer, reducing their separation from kiloparsecs (thousands of parsecs) to a few parsecs (tens of light-years). Binary Formation and Hardening (Intermediate Stage): Once the SMBHs are within a few parsecs of each other, they form a gravitationally bound binary system. At this stage, dynamical friction becomes less effective because the SMBHs have cleared out much of the surrounding material. The binary hardens through three-body interactions, where the SMBHs eject stars from the galactic center via gravitational slingshot effects, further reducing their separation to around 1 parsec. The Final Parsec Problem (Stalling Stage): At a separation of approximately 1 parsec, the binary’s orbital decay slows significantly or stalls. The problem arises because the mechanisms that were effective at larger separations—dynamical friction and stellar ejections—become inefficient. There are not enough stars left in the "loss cone" (the region where stars can interact closely with the binary) to extract sufficient energy and angular momentum to bring the SMBHs closer. Additionally, gravitational wave emission, which becomes the dominant mechanism for energy loss at very small separations (sub-parsec scales), is not yet strong enough at 1 parsec to drive the merger within a reasonable timescale (e.g., the age of the universe, ~13.8 billion years). Gravitational Wave Emission (Final Merger Stage): If the SMBHs can overcome the final parsec, they enter a regime where gravitational wave emission dominates, rapidly reducing their separation and leading to a merger. This stage produces detectable gravitational waves, as observed by experiments like LIGO and Virgo. The Challenge The final parsec problem is a challenge because theoretical models predict that many SMBH binaries should stall at separations of ~1 parsec, taking longer than the age of the universe to merge. However, observational evidence—such as the detection of gravitational waves from SMBH mergers and the presence of massive black holes in merged galaxies—suggests that these binaries do merge. The discrepancy between theory and observation indicates that additional mechanisms are needed to bridge the "final parsec" gap. Proposed Solutions in Astrophysics Several mechanisms have been proposed to solve the final parsec problem: Gas Dynamics: In gas-rich environments (e.g., during a "wet" merger), the SMBHs can interact with a circumbinary disk of gas, which extracts angular momentum through viscous dissipation, allowing the binary to shrink. Stellar Dynamics: In triaxial or non-spherical galaxies, the loss cone can be repopulated with stars on eccentric orbits, enabling continued three-body interactions to extract energy from the binary. Third Black Hole (Kozai-Lidov Mechanism): The presence of a third black hole can induce the Kozai-Lidov mechanism, where gravitational perturbations cause the binary’s orbit to become more eccentric, reducing the merger timescale. Dark Matter or Other Particles: Interactions with dark matter particles or other exotic particles could provide additional energy loss mechanisms. However, these mechanisms are not universally applicable, as they depend on the specific environment (e.g., gas-rich vs. gas-poor galaxies) and may not fully resolve the problem in all cases.________________________________________ Integration with the Superconductive Universe Framework In our framework, the final parsec problem (Drawing 3) is addressed through the dynamics of [SCm] and [UA], which provide a novel mechanism for energy and angular momentum extraction, independent of traditional gravitational wave emission or stellar dynamics. The study aims to quantify this effect using simulations and observations. (2023) continue the analysis of metal retention in the circumgalactic medium (CGM) of galaxies, focusing on the role of active galactic nucleus (AGN) feedback, the M–σ relation, and the implications for galaxy evolution. The authors compare simulation results with mock observations, discuss the impact of AGN feedback on metal and mass gradients, and provide predictions for future surveys. Key points include: AGN Feedback Flattens Mass and Metallicity Gradients (Pages 11–12): The authors find that galaxies with over-massive SMBHs (above the M–σ relation) have flatter metallicity gradients in their disks and CGM due to stronger AGN feedback, which drives metals out of the central regions. Galaxies with under-massive SMBHs retain more metals in their centers, leading to steeper gradients. Figure 7 shows gas-phase and stellar metallicity profiles, with over-massive SMBHs (red lines) having flatter profiles compared to under-massive SMBHs (blue lines). Gas and Stellar Mass Profiles (Page 12): Figure 8 compares gas and stellar mass profiles, showing that over-massive SMBHs have lower central gas masses due to ejection, while under-massive SMBHs retain more gas in their centers. Stellar mass profiles are similar for both groups, but under-massive SMBHs have more centrally concentrated stellar mass. CGM Baryon Fraction (Page 12): Figure 9 shows the CGM baryon fraction (fCGM=MCGM/MvirfCGM=MCGM/Mvir) as a function of ΔMBHΔMBH. Galaxies with over-massive SMBHs have lower fCGMfCGM, indicating that AGN feedback evacuates baryons from the CGM. Mock Observations of Metal Retention (Pages 12–13): Figure 10 compares simulated and observed metal retention fractions, showing that simulated galaxies have higher fZ,diskfZ,disk than observed galaxies, likely due to differences in disk definitions. Figure 11 shows the total metal mass formed in the disk, with simulations overestimating metal production compared to observations. Mock Observations of CGM Baryon Fraction (Page 13): Figure 12 compares the CGM baryon fraction in simulations and observations, finding that simulated galaxies have higher fCGMfCGM than observed, possibly due to differences in gas definitions. Column Densities of C IV (Pages 13–14): Figure 13 shows mock C IV column densities as a function of radius, with over-massive SMBHs having lower central C IV densities due to AGN-driven outflows. Figure 14 compares these with observed C IV column densities, noting discrepancies due to observational biases. Cumulative Accreted BH Mass (Page 14): Figure 15 plots the cumulative accreted SMBH mass over time, showing that over-massive SMBHs (red lines) grow earlier than under-massive SMBHs (blue lines), impacting metal retention. Predictions for Future CGM Surveys (Page 14): The authors predict that future surveys like COS-Holes will detect differences in C IV column densities between over- and under-massive SMBHs, with over-massive SMBHs showing lower central C IV due to AGN feedback. AGN Feedback Does Not Evacuate Gas from the CGM (Pages 14–15): The authors find that AGN feedback does not significantly evacuate gas from the CGM, as fCGMfCGM does not correlate strongly with ΔMBHΔMBH. Instead, AGN feedback redistributes metals within the CGM. BHs Primarily Drive Metals into the CGM, Not the IGM (Pages 15–16): Over-massive SMBHs drive metals into the CGM rather than the intergalactic medium (IGM), as shown in Figures 7–9. Under-massive SMBHs retain metals in the disk, with less ejection into the CGM. Mock Observations of Metal Retention (Pages 16–17): The authors create mock observations for metal retention, finding that simulated galaxies overestimate metal retention compared to observations, likely due to differences in disk definitions. Column Densities of C IV (Pages 17–18): The authors predict C IV column densities for future surveys, noting that over-massive SMBHs will show lower central C IV due to AGN-driven outflows. Predictions for Future CGM Surveys (Page 18): Future surveys will help determine whether SMBHs evacuate gas from the CGM, with implications for galaxy evolution. References (Pages 18–20): The authors provide a bibliography supporting their findings, including works on cosmological simulations, AGN feedback, and metal retention.
